newsitem.title: USA: Grigsby Brandford says in solid condition.
newsitem.headline: Grigsby Brandford says in solid condition.

text.p: Investment banking firm Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc said on Thursday the firm maintains a solid financial condition and is moving forward with new business following the resignation of its chairman.
The firm said in a statement that it was in the process of restructuring its partnership interest.
As of August 31, the firm's net capital was $5.4 million, which included $3.1 million subordinated debt irrevocably pledged to the firm through October 1999.
"We also have a significant pipeline of deals into 1997," the firm said in the statement.

"All of our major clients have indicated a desire to continue our service and, moreover, no significant clients have indicated an unwillingness to move forward with us," the firm said. "We are confident that over the next weeks and months Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc will continue to demonstrate its solid position and contribution to the municipal marketplace."

The firm said it would have no comment on its former chairman, Calvin Grigsby, or his resignation earlier this month, "except to say that we have both chosen paths of separate and chellenging responsibilities."

In a separate statement, Grigsby Brandford said it served as book-running senior manager and received the verbal award for $32.6 million of certificates of participation sold for the city of Hayward, Calif., civic center project.

In addition, it closed two transactions as sole manager. They included a $6.5 million Richmond Joint Powers Financing Authority port terminal lease revenue bonds, and $1.5 million Lynwood Public Financing Authority lease revenue bonds.
On September 17, Grigsby resigned as chairman of the firm, which is one of the nation's largest minority-owned investment banking firms.
The Miami Herald newspaper reported last week that Grigsby resigned after federal prosecutors from Miami interviewed him in California about Dade County, Fla., bond deals.
The Herald reported Thursday that FBI videotapes show Dade County Commissioner James Burke discussing a $300,000 kickback with Grigsby in exchange for steering bond business to Grigsby's firm.

Grigsby's resignation also came a week after the California Fair Political Practices Commission disclosed that Grigsby paid a $5,000 fine for making campaign contributions in California without full and complete disclosure.
Earlier this week, a Securities and Exchange Commission official in Florida asked the California commission for its campaign contribution files on Grigsby, sources said.
The move suggests that the SEC staff in Miami has launched a probe of bond deals in Dade County involving Grigsby.
Charles Senatore, the SEC's regional director in Miami, declined to comment. An SEC official in California also declined to comment.
Grigsby could not be reached for comment.
